title: resume() re-persists pre-recovery state, undoing recover_dispatched_steps()
evidence:
`resume()` loads a state object, then calls a recovery method that loads and saves a *different* object, then writes the stale first object back:

```python
state = self._load_execution()          # 4740 — object A, still has status="dispatched"
...
self.recover_dispatched_steps()          # 4820 — loads object B, strips dispatched, saves B
...
action = self._drive_resolver_loop(state)  # 4833 — drives stale object A
self._save_execution(state)                # 4834 — writes A back: recovery erased
```

`recover_dispatched_steps()` (4838) does `state = self._load_execution()` itself and `self._save_execution(state)` on its own object. `_load_execution()` (798) deserializes a fresh `ExecutionState` on every call — there is no in-memory cache — so A and B are distinct objects. The clobbering save was introduced by commit fefb490 ("resume() saves execution state after the resolver loop, mirroring siblings").

Live reproduction: `pytest tests/test_phase0_resume_recovery.py` → 2 failed, 2 passed, with `AssertionError: resume() must clear steps stuck in 'dispatched' status / assert '1.1' not in {'1.1'}`. Direct probe: after start + mark_dispatched + fresh-engine `resume()`, the action is `ActionType.WAIT — "Waiting for in-flight steps to complete before proceeding."` and persisted step statuses are `[('1.1', 'dispatched')]`.
why_it_matters: This is the documented crash-recovery path (`baton execute resume` in root CLAUDE.md: "If the session crashes, `baton execute resume` picks up from saved state"). After a crash mid-dispatch, the agent process is gone but its StepResult stays `dispatched`. The resolver puts `dispatched_step_ids` into its `occupied` set (resolver.py:319-325), so the step is never re-dispatched and the `pending` set is non-empty → permanent `ACTION: wait`. Every subsequent `resume`/`next` repeats it. The state file is actively rewritten with the stale marker, so the corruption is durable, not transient. This exactly reproduces the symptom already filed as BUG-002 in docs/baton-engine-bugs.md ("stuck in ACTION: wait ... engine never advances"). Two regression tests written specifically to prevent this are red in the repo right now.
proposed_fix: Make `recover_dispatched_steps()` operate on a caller-supplied state, or have `resume()` re-read after recovery. Minimal fix: change the signature to `recover_dispatched_steps(self, state: ExecutionState | None = None) -> int` — when `state` is passed, mutate it in place and skip the internal load/save (the caller's save covers it); when `None`, keep today's load/save behaviour for `WorkerSupervisor` (core/runtime/supervisor.py:149). Then `resume()` calls `self.recover_dispatched_steps(state)` before `_drive_resolver_loop(state)`. Add a defensive assertion/log if `_drive_resolver_loop` is ever handed a state whose `_loaded_version` is behind the persisted version.
test_strategy: tests/test_phase0_resume_recovery.py already encodes the assertions and must go green: after start → `mark_dispatched('1.1')` → fresh `ExecutionEngine.resume()`, (a) the *persisted* state must contain no StepResult with `status == 'dispatched'`, and (b) `resume()`'s own return value must be `ActionType.DISPATCH` with `step_id == '1.1'` — not WAIT. Add the missing assertion on resume()'s return action (the current test only checks the follow-up `next_action()`). Add a case with a completed step + a dispatched step to prove the completed result survives the recovery save.

title: record_gate_result() validates nothing — a gate pass for any phase_id advances the phase and skips un-run steps
evidence:
`record_gate_result` performs no pre-condition checks at all. It reads gate_type from whatever phase happens to be current, not from the phase being recorded:

```python
state = self._require_execution("record_gate_result")
phase_obj = state.current_phase_obj                       # 3638 — NOT resolved by phase_id
gate_type = phase_obj.gate.gate_type if (phase_obj and phase_obj.gate) else "unknown"
...
else:                                                      # passed
    ...
    self._phase_manager.advance_phase(state, set_status_running=True)   # 3832 — unconditional
```

Compare the sibling `record_approval_result` (4914-4990), which carries four explicit "Hole 1 validations": status must be `approval_pending`, `phase_id` must match `current_phase_obj.phase_id`, the phase must have `approval_required=True`, and team-mode self-approval is blocked — each raising `InvalidApprovalState`. None of that exists for gates, and the CLI passes `args.phase_id` straight through (execute.py:1209) with no validation.

Probe 1 — plan with phase 1 (gate, steps 1.1 + 1.2) and phase 2; immediately after `start()` (status `running`, zero steps run) `record_gate_result(phase_id=1, passed=True)` yields `status: running, current_phase: 1, step_results: []` and the next action is `DISPATCH 2.1`. Steps 1.1 and 1.2 are skipped permanently.

Probe 2 — `record_gate_result(phase_id=99, passed=True)` on a 2-phase plan: accepted, stored as `GateResult(phase_id=99, gate_type='test', passed=True)` (gate_type stolen from phase 1), `current_phase` advanced to 1, next action `DISPATCH 2.1`. No exception, no warning.
why_it_matters: A single mistyped or out-of-order `baton execute gate --phase-id N --result pass` silently discards an entire phase of planned work, and the QA gate the phase depended on is recorded as passed against a phase that may not exist. The engine's whole value proposition is a deterministic state machine with enforced QA gates; this makes the gate record forgeable by accident. It is also an assurance-trail defect: `GateResult.gate_type`/`derived_commands`/`agent_additions` are all derived from `current_phase_obj` rather than the recorded phase, so evidence bundles for regulated runs can carry a gate_type that belongs to a different phase. The repo's own guiding principle 5 ("could this be failing silently") is violated: there is no error, no log, and no test — `grep -c record_gate_result tests/` finds zero phase-mismatch tests.
proposed_fix: Mirror the approval guards. At the top of `record_gate_result`: (1) resolve `phase = next((p for p in state.plan.phases if p.phase_id == phase_id), None)` and raise a typed error from `engine/errors.py` (e.g. a new `InvalidGateState` with reasons `unknown_phase` / `phase_mismatch` / `not_pending` / `no_gate`) when it is None; (2) require `phase is state.current_phase_obj`; (3) require `phase.gate is not None`; (4) require `state.status in ('gate_pending', 'gate_failed', 'running')` and, for `passed=True`, require `is_phase_complete(state, phase_id)` from `_executor_helpers` so a pass can never jump over un-run steps; (5) derive `gate_type`, `command`, and the extension provenance from `phase`, not `state.current_phase_obj`. Map the new exception to a clean CLI `user_error` in execute.py alongside the existing `UnknownTeamBackendError` handler.
test_strategy: Assert that `record_gate_result(phase_id=<non-current>, passed=True)` and `record_gate_result(phase_id=99, ...)` both raise the typed error and leave `state.current_phase`, `state.gate_results`, and `state.status` byte-identical to before the call. Assert that `record_gate_result(phase_id=<current>, passed=True)` while any step of that phase is still non-terminal raises rather than advancing. Assert the happy path (all steps complete, status gate_pending) still advances exactly one phase and stamps `GateResult.gate_type` from the *recorded* phase's gate when `current_phase_obj` has a different gate type.

title: Investigative RETRY_PHASE loop-back never re-runs anything — it burns the retry budget and advances
evidence:
`PhaseManager.retry_phase` resets an index and a counter but never clears the phase's results:

```python
retry_store[retry_key] = int(retry_store.get(retry_key, 0)) + 1
state.current_step_index = sum(len(p.steps) for p in state.plan.phases[:state.current_phase])
state.status = "running"
```

But the resolver never consults `current_step_index`. Step selection is driven entirely by result status (resolver.py:312-336): `occupied = completed | failed | dispatched | interrupted | interacting`, and `completed_step_ids` is a computed property over `step_results` (models/execution.py:1511). Since `retry_phase` leaves every StepResult at `status="complete"`, the phase's steps stay in `occupied` and the dispatch scan finds nothing.

Probe (2-phase investigative plan, `max_retry_phases=3`, step 1.1 complete with `outcome="falsified RETRY_PHASE"`), looping resolver → `phase_manager.retry_phase`:
```
0 RETRY_PHASE  phase=0 idx=0 retries={}
1 RETRY_PHASE  phase=0 idx=0 retries={'phase_1': 1}
2 RETRY_PHASE  phase=0 idx=0 retries={'phase_1': 2}
3 PHASE_ADVANCE_OK phase=0 idx=0 retries={'phase_1': 3}
```
No DISPATCH is ever produced. `_apply_resolver_decision`'s RETRY_PHASE arm (6852-6860) only logs and returns `None` to loop, so the three retries are consumed inside a single `_drive_resolver_loop` call and the phase advances as if nothing happened.

The feature is instructed to agents by the planner: decomposition.py:432 injects "If hypothesis is falsified, include 'RETRY_PHASE' in output to loop back".
why_it_matters: The investigative archetype (auto-selected for debugging tasks, `max_retry_phases=3` hardcoded in planning/stages/assembly.py:106) tells the agent it can loop back when a hypothesis is falsified. It cannot. An agent that correctly reports a falsified hypothesis gets its signal acknowledged with a log line and the plan marches on to "Fix" and "Verify" phases built on a disproven hypothesis. Nothing surfaces to the user — no bead, no action, no CLI output — so the failure is entirely silent (guiding principle 5). It also risks the `_drive_resolver_loop` bound: retries consume iterations from `max_iter = len(state.plan.phases) + 4` (executor.py:6375), so raising `max_retry_phases` above that margin turns a no-op into a hard `RuntimeError`.
proposed_fix: Make `retry_phase` actually reset the phase: drop every `StepResult` whose `step_id` belongs to the current phase (`state.step_results = [r for r in state.step_results if r.step_id not in {s.step_id for s in phase.steps}]`), and drop that phase's `gate_results`/`approval_results`/`feedback_results` so the phase gate re-runs. Preserve the removed results in an audit list (or write a bead) so token spend and prior outcomes are not lost — `estimated_tokens` on discarded results currently vanishes from the budget sum in resolver.py:248. Guard the retry counter check so `max_retry_phases` can never exceed the resolver-loop bound, and emit a phase-retry domain event so the retry is visible in the trace.
test_strategy: Given an investigative plan whose only phase has one completed step with `outcome` containing 'RETRY_PHASE', driving `ExecutionEngine.next_action()` must return `ActionType.DISPATCH` for that same step_id (not COMPLETE), and `state.phase_retries['phase_1'] == 1`. After `max_retry_phases` retries the engine must advance exactly once and the total number of DISPATCH actions for that step must equal `max_retry_phases + 1`. Also assert the accumulated `estimated_tokens` across retries is not lost from the budget total.

title: Policy-block APPROVAL is unresolvable: no CLI/API surface, in-memory-only unblock, and the reject path writes to a computed property
evidence:
`_check_policy_block` returns an APPROVAL action with the sentinel `phase_id=-1` (1737-1752) but never touches `state.status` — the execution stays `running`. The only handler, `record_policy_approval` (1760), stores the unblock in a per-process set:

```python
self._policy_approved_steps: set[str] = set()   # 497 — never persisted
...
if result == "approve":
    self._policy_approved_steps.add(step_id)
```

and its reject arm writes to a computed property:

```python
state.failed_step_ids.add(step_id)   # 1786 — no-op
state.transition_to_failed()
```

`ExecutionState.failed_step_ids` is a `@property` returning a freshly built set (`{r.step_id for r in self.step_results if r.status == "failed"}`, models/execution.py:1515) — confirmed at runtime: `type(ExecutionState.failed_step_ids) is property`. `.add()` mutates a throwaway.

`grep -rn record_policy_approval agent_baton/` finds hits only inside executor.py — no CLI subcommand and no API route call it. Meanwhile `_print_action` prints the generic APPROVAL block telling the operator to run `baton execute approve --phase-id -1 --result approve`, which routes to `record_approval_result` and hits Hole-1 validation #1 (`status != 'approval_pending'`) → `InvalidApprovalState`.

This is a known, still-open defect: docs/reviews/system-audit-roadmap.md:56 files it as C03 and docs/reviews/audit-01-core-engine-execution.md:100 describes the same no-op.
why_it_matters: Two compounding failures. (1) When a guardrail preset blocks a step, the orchestrator gets an APPROVAL it cannot satisfy from the CLI: the printed command raises, `record_policy_approval` is unreachable, and even a direct Python call is lost because `_policy_approved_steps` dies with the process — so the very next `baton execute next` re-emits the same APPROVAL. Policy enforcement is a hard stop with no exit. (2) On reject, `transition_to_failed()` does run, so execution ends as `failed`, but no StepResult carries `status='failed'`. The resolver's terminal-failed message then reads `failed_ids = sorted(state.failed_step_ids)` → empty → `joined = ", ".join(failed_ids) or "gate"` (resolver.py:168-170), so the operator is told "Execution failed. Failed step(s): gate" for a policy rejection that had nothing to do with a gate. Evidence bundles and retrospectives inherit the same lie.
proposed_fix: (a) Replace `state.failed_step_ids.add(step_id)` with an appended `StepResult(step_id=step_id, agent_name=..., status='failed', error='policy rejection: <rule names>', completed_at=_utcnow())` before `transition_to_failed()`. (b) Persist the unblock: store approved step_ids on `ExecutionState` (e.g. `policy_approved_step_ids`) instead of the per-process set, and have `_check_policy_block` read from state. (c) Expose the decision: add `baton execute policy-approve --step-id X --result approve|reject` (or route `approve --phase-id -1` to `record_policy_approval`, reading the step_id the action already embeds in `summary`), and print that exact command from `_print_action` when `phase_id == -1`.
test_strategy: With a policy engine whose preset blocks a step: assert `next_action()` returns APPROVAL with `phase_id == -1`; assert `record_policy_approval(step_id, 'approve')` followed by a *fresh* `ExecutionEngine` on the same context root returns DISPATCH for that step (proves persistence); assert `record_policy_approval(step_id, 'reject')` produces a `StepResult` with `status == 'failed'` for that step_id and that the subsequent FAILED action's message names the step, not 'gate'. Add a CLI test that the command string printed for a `phase_id == -1` APPROVAL actually succeeds when executed.

title: _print_action has no WAIT or CHECKPOINT branch — emits lowercase keywords contrary to the documented protocol; CHECKPOINT is dead protocol surface
evidence:
`_print_action` branches on DISPATCH, GATE, APPROVAL, FEEDBACK, COMPLETE, FAILED and INTERACT, then falls through:

```python
    else:
        print(f"ACTION: {atype}")   # execute.py:803 — atype is the raw enum *value*
        print(f"  {msg}")
```

`ActionType.WAIT = "wait"` and `ActionType.CHECKPOINT = "checkpoint"` (models/execution.py:68,72) are lowercase, so the emitted lines are `ACTION: wait` / `ACTION: checkpoint`. Verified by running `_print_action(ExecutionAction(action_type=ActionType.WAIT, ...).to_dict())` → `ACTION: wait`.

The contract docs specify uppercase: docs/invariants.md:79 shows `ACTION: WAIT\n  Message: <description>` and :94 shows `ACTION: CHECKPOINT\n  Message: <description>`; references/baton-engine.md:1919 (the agent-side protocol contract this domain's CLAUDE.md mandates keeping in sync) also documents `ACTION: WAIT`. The function's own docstring calls itself "**PUBLIC API** ... The orchestrator reads stdout line-by-line and keys on the exact field labels" and lists changes to action-type keywords as "a **breaking change**".

Separately, `grep -rn 'ActionType.CHECKPOINT' agent_baton/` returns nothing — no code path anywhere constructs a CHECKPOINT action, yet it is enumerated in docs/architecture/state-machine.md:30 and docs/invariants.md:94 as part of the emitted protocol.

`grep -rn _print_action tests/` shows coverage for DISPATCH, FEEDBACK and terse mode only — no WAIT or CHECKPOINT case.
why_it_matters: WAIT is a routinely emitted action in parallel/`next_actions` mode and on the crash-resume path. An orchestrator agent implemented against the documented contract (matching `ACTION: WAIT`) silently fails to recognise it and falls into an unknown-action path — precisely the class of breakage the docstring and engine/CLAUDE.md's protocol-change discipline exist to prevent. CHECKPOINT is worse than drift: it is a documented capability ("save state and suggest a fresh session to prevent context rot") that the engine can never produce, so a user reading state-machine.md has no way to obtain the behaviour they were told exists (guiding principle 7).
proposed_fix: Add explicit `elif atype == ActionType.WAIT.value:` and `elif atype == ActionType.CHECKPOINT.value:` branches emitting `ACTION: WAIT` / `ACTION: CHECKPOINT` with the `Message:` label the docs specify, and make the terminal `else` uppercase (`print(f"ACTION: {atype.upper()}")`) so any future ActionType degrades to the documented casing. Then either implement a CHECKPOINT emitter (e.g. a turn/token-count threshold in `_drive_resolver_loop`) or remove CHECKPOINT from `ActionType` and from docs/invariants.md + docs/architecture/state-machine.md — per engine/CLAUDE.md that removal is a coordinated protocol change across agents/orchestrator.md, references/baton-engine.md and docs/design-decisions.md.
test_strategy: A parametrised test over all nine `ActionType` values asserting the first stdout line of `_print_action` is exactly `ACTION: <NAME>` where `<NAME> == member.name` (uppercase) — this fails today for WAIT and CHECKPOINT and locks the invariant for future members. Plus a test asserting the WAIT block includes the `Message:` label as documented in docs/invariants.md:79. For CHECKPOINT, either an emission test (engine returns a CHECKPOINT action under the threshold condition) or a static test asserting every `ActionType` member is constructed somewhere in `agent_baton/`.

title: ExecutionDriver.record_gate_result docstring contradicts the implementation on gate failure ('failed' vs 'gate_failed')
evidence:
The 15-method `ExecutionDriver` contract states:

```python
def record_gate_result(self, phase_id: int, passed: bool, output: str = "") -> None:
    """...
    On failure, sets execution status to ``failed``.  On success,
    advances the phase pointer to the next phase.
```

The implementation's own docstring repeats it (executor.py:3620 "If *failed*: sets state status to ``failed``"), but every failure branch actually writes `gate_failed`:

```python
state.status = "gate_failed"  # noqa: state-mutation   # 3786 and 3810
```

`gate_failed` is a distinct, *recoverable* status: the resolver's `gate_failed` arm (resolver.py:205-231) counts prior failures and returns `GATE_FAILED` (retryable) until `fail_count >= max_gate_retries`, and two public methods exist purely to service it — `reset_gate_failed` (3864) requires `status == 'gate_failed'` and `fail_gate` (3902) is what actually performs the `failed` transition. The implementation signature has also grown four parameters (`command`, `exit_code`, `decision_source`, `actor`) that the protocol does not declare.
why_it_matters: `protocols.py` is called out in engine/CLAUDE.md as "the seam between async runtime and the synchronous engine" and "the most critical contract in the system" — an alternative `ExecutionDriver` implementation (the doc explicitly invites one for testing or alternative runtimes) written to this contract would flip straight to `failed` on the first gate failure, destroying the retry/`reset_gate_failed`/`fail_gate` state cluster and every `BATON_GATE_RETRY` behaviour. A caller reading the contract also has no way to learn that `retry-gate` is available after a failure (guiding principle 7). The undeclared kwargs mean a conforming implementation would break `record_gate_result(..., decision_source=..., actor=...)` calls the CLI makes for the A2/A6 assurance trail.
proposed_fix: Update the `ExecutionDriver.record_gate_result` docstring to: "On failure, sets execution status to `gate_failed` — a recoverable state; the caller may retry via `reset_gate_failed(phase_id)` or terminate via `fail_gate(phase_id)`. After `max_gate_retries` failures the resolver escalates to a terminal FAILED action." Add the four missing parameters to the protocol signature (or document them as implementation extensions). Fix the same sentence in executor.py:3620. Per engine/CLAUDE.md this is a protocol-doc change, so mirror it in references/baton-engine.md and docs/architecture/state-machine.md.
test_strategy: A contract test asserting that after `record_gate_result(phase_id=<current>, passed=False)` the persisted `state.status == 'gate_failed'` (never `'failed'`) and that `reset_gate_failed(phase_id)` succeeds from that status; plus a static/doc test (in the spirit of tests/static/test_no_direct_status_writes.py) asserting the `ExecutionDriver.record_gate_result` docstring does not claim status `failed` and that its parameter set is a subset of `ExecutionEngine.record_gate_result`'s via `inspect.signature`.

title: Investigative-archetype tasks are unplannable — every plan is hard-blocked by review_missing
evidence: `_build_investigative_phases` hard-codes a `code-reviewer` into a phase named `Verify` (decomposition.py:474-479: `name="Verify", steps=[PlanStep(step_id="4.1", agent_name="code-reviewer", ...)]`). ValidationStage then requires review coverage whenever any reviewer-class agent is on the plan (`_review_required`, validation.py:485-489: `or bool(agent_bases & self._REVIEWER_BASES)`) but only accepts it from a phase whose key is literally `review` (`_has_review_coverage`, validation.py:503-509: `if self._phase_key(phase.name) != "review": continue`). `_phase_key("Verify")` returns `"verify"`, so coverage is never found. The archetype branch also returns early at decomposition.py:107-124 without ever consulting `draft.classified_phases`, so RiskStage's compensating fix-up (risk.py:281-300, which appends a `Review` slot when a reviewer is on the roster) is bypassed on this path. Reproduced deterministically with the keyword classifier: `IntelligentPlanner(task_classifier=KeywordClassifier()).create_plan("Debug the intermittent 500 error in the checkout API")` raises `PlanQualityError: ... [critical] review_missing`. Same for "Add a null check to the parser to avoid the exception". The trigger regex `_INVESTIGATIVE_SIGNALS` (classifier.py:192-199) matches `debug|investigate|diagnose|root.?cause|triage|regression|flaky|intermittent|exception|crash|traceback|reproduce|symptom`, so the blast radius is most debugging work.
why_it_matters: `baton plan "Investigate the failing regression in the reporting module"` exits with PlanQualityError and produces no plan. Debugging/RCA — one of the headline use cases and the reason the investigative archetype exists — is 100% unusable. Setting BATON_DEV_MODE=1 does not rescue it: the plan then fails a second way (see the consolidate_team_step finding) with a pydantic ValidationError.
proposed_fix: Make `_has_review_coverage` accept the archetype's terminal review-type phase: derive the accepted keys from a table (e.g. `{"review", "verify", "audit"}` or `ArchetypeConfig`) rather than the single literal `"review"`, and mirror the same table in `_phase_key`/`PHASE_IDEAL_ROLES`. Additionally, run the archetype branch's output through the same safety-roster/phase reconciliation the phased path gets — either move `_ensure_safety_roster`'s classified_phases fix-up to operate on built phases, or have `_build_investigative_phases` name its terminal phase `Review` and keep 'Verify' as a display label.
test_strategy: End-to-end: `IntelligentPlanner(task_classifier=KeywordClassifier()).create_plan("Debug the intermittent 500 error in the checkout API")` must return a MachinePlan (not raise), with `plan.archetype == "investigative"`, four phases, and `ValidationStage()._detect_defects(draft)` returning no `review_missing` defect. Parameterise over at least three investigative trigger words. A unit test must also assert `_has_review_coverage` returns True for a phase named `Verify` carrying a `code-reviewer` step.

title: ForesightEngine renumbers step ids without rewriting depends_on — dependency edges silently re-point at the wrong step
evidence: foresight.py:388-393 renumbers every phase and step after inserting a Prepare phase: `phase.phase_id = next_phase_id` / `for i, step in enumerate(phase.steps, start=1): step.step_id = f"{next_phase_id}.{i}"`. Nothing in `analyze()` touches `step.depends_on`. Reproduced: feeding phases `[Investigate(1.1), Fix(2.1 depends_on=["1.1"])]` with a migration-rollback trigger through `ForesightEngine().analyze(...)` returns `Prepare: Migration Safety(1.1)`, `Investigate(2.1)`, `Fix(3.1, depends_on=['1.1'])` — the Fix step now depends on the *inserted Prepare step* instead of the Investigate step, and the Investigate step has no dependents. The plan is still structurally valid (1.1 is an earlier step), so no exception is raised and no warning is logged. DecompositionStage calls this on every plan (`_apply_foresight`, decomposition.py:269-303) and the only intra-plan `depends_on` edges the planner produces are the archetype ones (decomposition.py:374, 436, 452, 463, 486) — exactly the ones foresight scrambles.
why_it_matters: An investigative/direct plan with a foresight insertion executes with a silently wrong dependency graph: the Fix step is gated on tooling provisioning rather than on the investigation that identifies the root cause, so it can be dispatched before its actual prerequisite completes. Nothing surfaces — no exception, no log line, no defect. This is precisely the 'could this be failing silently' failure mode the repo's guiding principles call out.
proposed_fix: Build an old-id → new-id map while renumbering and rewrite every `step.depends_on` entry through it as a final pass in `analyze()` (and mirror the same remap for `PlanPhase`-level references if any are added later). Any dependency that cannot be mapped should be dropped with an explicit `logger.warning`, not silently retained.
test_strategy: Unit test on `ForesightEngine.analyze`: given phases `[P1(step 1.1), P2(step 2.1 depends_on=['1.1'])]` and a task summary that fires the migration-rollback rule, assert the returned Fix step's `depends_on == ['2.1']` (the renumbered Investigate step) and that no returned step depends on an inserted foresight step id. Add a property-style assertion that for every returned step, each `depends_on` id resolves to a step whose original identity is unchanged.

title: consolidate_team_step drops step ids without remapping dependents, producing an unconstructible MachinePlan
evidence: `consolidate_team_step` collapses all of a phase's steps into one step whose id is `f"{phase.phase_id}.1"` (phase_builder.py:688-695) and drops the source steps' ids and their `depends_on` entirely. ValidationStage applies it unconditionally to any Implement/Fix phase with >=2 steps (validation.py:279-283 + `is_team_phase`, phase_builder.py:620-632). Instrumented run of the investigative plan under `BATON_PLANNER_WARN_ONLY=1` shows the Fix phase collapsing `3.1`+`3.2` into a single `3.1` team step while the Verify step still carries `depends_on=['3.2']`, and AssemblyStage then dies: `pydantic ValidationError ... Plan-graph invariant violation: step '4.1' depends on '3.2', which is not declared as an earlier step.`
why_it_matters: Any plan where a later step depends on the second-or-later step of a consolidated Implement/Fix phase cannot be constructed at all — `create_plan` raises a raw pydantic ValidationError with no actionable remediation (unlike PlanQualityError, which carries a Remediation string). Today this is the second failure mode of every investigative plan; it will fire for any future template that adds cross-phase edges into a multi-agent implement phase.
proposed_fix: Have `consolidate_team_step` return the id mapping (each source step id → the new team step id / the member id that absorbed it) and have the ValidationStage caller rewrite `depends_on` across the whole plan through that map before the reviewer pass. Also carry the union of the source steps' `depends_on` onto the consolidated step, which is currently dropped outright.
test_strategy: Given a plan with a Fix phase containing steps 3.1 and 3.2 and a later step 4.1 with `depends_on=['3.2']`, run ValidationStage and assert (a) the Fix phase has one team step 3.1 with two members, (b) step 4.1's `depends_on == ['3.1']`, and (c) `MachinePlan(...)` constructs without raising. Also assert the consolidated step inherits the union of its source steps' depends_on.

title: Structured-spec plans hard-block when only some phases name an agent
evidence: `phases_from_dicts` only falls back to `assign_agents_to_phases` when *every* phase came out empty: `all_steps_empty = all(not p.steps for p in phases); if all_steps_empty and agents: return assign_agents_to_phases(...)` (phase_builder.py:421-425). `parse_structured_description` routinely returns a partial parse — for the summary "Phase 1: Authentication - implement OAuth callback / Phase 2: Authorization - token validation and RBAC / Phase 3: Review - security review of the flow" it returns `[{'name':'Phase 1','agents':[]}, {'name':'Phase 2','agents':[]}, {'name':'Phase 3','agents':['security-reviewer']}]`. Because one phase has an agent, the guard is skipped, phases 1 and 2 stay empty, and ValidationStage's `empty_phase` detector (validation.py:426-440) blocks the plan: `PlanQualityError: ... [critical] empty_phase: phase_id=1 ... step_count=0; [critical] empty_phase: phase_id=2 ... step_count=0`.
why_it_matters: The structured-spec path is the entry point for Spec Federation imports and for operators pasting a phased spec into `baton plan`. Any spec where one phase happens to mention a role name (very common — 'Review', 'security review', 'QA') and the others do not is rejected outright with a defect message that blames the plan rather than the parser. The operator's documented workaround (per structured_spec.py's own docstring, this loss of information is what makes operators 'bypass the planner and dispatch each spec line manually') is exactly the failure mode this module was written to prevent.
proposed_fix: Change the rescue in `phases_from_dicts` from all-or-nothing to per-phase: after building, fill any phase with zero steps via `assign_agents_to_phases` (or the `PHASE_FALLBACK_AGENT` table) rather than only when every phase is empty.
test_strategy: `phases_from_dicts([{'name':'Phase 1','agents':[]},{'name':'Phase 2','agents':[]},{'name':'Phase 3','agents':['security-reviewer']}], ['backend-engineer','security-reviewer'], summary, registry)` must return three phases each with >=1 step. End-to-end: `create_plan` on the three-line OAuth spec above must return a MachinePlan and `_detect_defects` must contain no `empty_phase`.

title: _phase_key misparses structured-spec phase names, silently disabling every phase↔role guard
evidence: `_phase_key` takes the text before the first colon and then its last word: `raw = (name or "").lower().split(":")[0].strip(); key = raw.split()[-1] if raw else ""` (validation.py:529-536). `enrich_phase_titles` deliberately produces names of the form `f"Phase {idx}: {title}"` (structured_spec.py:105-109), so `_phase_key("Phase 1: Authentication")` returns `"1"`. Every consumer keys off that string: `PHASE_BLOCKED_ROLES.get(phase_key, set())` (validation.py:451), `if phase_key in self._IMPLEMENT_PHASE_KEYS` (validation.py:466), `_has_review_coverage` (validation.py:505), `_has_audit_coverage` (validation.py:512). All miss. Reproduced: planning the spec 'Phase 1: Authentication with architect and backend-engineer / Phase 2: Authorization with backend-engineer and code-reviewer' yields phase 2 with steps `('2.1','backend-engineer')` and `('2.2','code-reviewer')` — a reviewer-class agent sitting as a plain implementer, i.e. the exact bd-1974 defect PHASE_BLOCKED_ROLES exists to block — and `_detect_defects` reports no `agent_phase_mismatch`. `_phase_key` for those phases prints `'1'` and `'2'`.
why_it_matters: Spec-derived plans — the ones that come from the Spec Queue / Federation importers and get the least human phase-by-phase scrutiny — run with all four phase-role guards silently inert. Architects land on implementation phases and reviewers review their own implementation work, with no defect, no warning, and a validation stage that reports a clean bill of health. The gate reports 'passed' precisely where it is not checking anything.
proposed_fix: Make `_phase_key` strip a leading `phase|step|stage|milestone <number>` prefix and key off the *title* segment after the colon, falling back to the pre-colon token only when no title exists. Add a defensive branch: when the derived key is purely numeric (or otherwise not in the known phase vocabulary), emit an `info`/`warning` defect ('phase name not classifiable — role guards not applied') so the gap is visible instead of silent.
test_strategy: Unit: `_phase_key("Phase 2: Authorization") == "authorization"` and `_phase_key("Phase 1: Implement OAuth") == "implement"`. Behavioural: build a draft with a phase named `"Phase 2: Implement"` containing an `architect` step and assert `_detect_defects` yields an `agent_phase_mismatch`; build one named `"Phase 3: Review"` with a `code-reviewer` step and assert `_has_review_coverage` is True.

title: Direct/investigative archetype builders take resolved_agents[0] raw, bypassing phase-role routing
evidence: `_build_direct_phases` assigns the implementer with `implement_agent = draft.resolved_agents[0] if draft.resolved_agents else "backend-engineer"` (decomposition.py:353); `_build_investigative_phases` does the same twice (decomposition.py:394-395). Neither calls `assign_agents_to_phases`, so `PHASE_IDEAL_ROLES`, `PHASE_BLOCKED_ROLES` (`{"implement": {"architect", "ai-systems-architect"}}`, phase_roles.py:37-40) and `PHASE_FALLBACK_AGENT` are all skipped — unlike every non-archetype path, which routes through `assign_agents_to_phases` (decomposition.py:158, 168). Reproduced deterministically: `create_plan("Rename one config flag in the settings module", task_classifier=KeywordClassifier())` → `[('Implement', ['immune-untested-edges']), ('Review', ['code-reviewer'])]`. `immune-untested-edges` is a registered immune-system *sweep* agent (agents/immune-untested-edges.md, 'Immune system sweep agent … scans a target file for calls to symbols marked @deprecated'), not an implementer; it won the classifier's keyword score and was taken as position 0 with no role check.
why_it_matters: A trivial rename gets dispatched to a specialised code-sweep agent as its sole implementer — the work simply will not get done, and there is no gate that notices because the archetype path skips the role tables. If `resolved_agents[0]` is instead `architect` (a common position-0 for new-feature rosters), the same path lands an architect in an Implement phase, which ValidationStage *does* catch — turning a routing bug into a hard PlanQualityError. Either outcome is produced by the same missing routing call.
proposed_fix: Have both archetype builders construct bare `PlanPhase` shells and run them through `assign_agents_to_phases(plan_phases, resolved_agents, task_summary, registry)`, or at minimum select the implementer as the first roster entry whose base is not in `PHASE_BLOCKED_ROLES["implement"]` and is in `PHASE_IDEAL_ROLES["implement"]`, falling back to `IMPLEMENT_FALLBACK_AGENT`.
test_strategy: Unit on `_build_direct_phases` with `draft.resolved_agents = ["architect", "backend-engineer"]`: assert the Implement step's agent base is not in `PHASE_BLOCKED_ROLES["implement"]`. With `["immune-untested-edges", "backend-engineer"]`: assert the Implement step resolves to `backend-engineer`. End-to-end assert `create_plan("Rename one config flag in the settings module")` never yields an `immune-*` agent as an Implement-phase step.

title: PlanReviewer's recommendation path is dead code — two documented ValidationStage defect detectors can never fire, and review failures are swallowed at debug level
evidence: `PlanReviewResult.warnings` is assigned in exactly one place — `result.warnings = recommendations.get("warnings", [])` at plan_reviewer.py:277, inside `_apply_recommendations`, which has no callers anywhere in `agent_baton/` (only `_heuristic_review` is reachable from `review()`, plan_reviewer.py:110-116). The same is true of `result.dependencies_added` (plan_reviewer.py:274). Consequently ValidationStage defect #7 `reviewer_warning`, which scans `getattr(review, "warnings", None) or []` for `[critical]` prefixes (validation.py:361-370), is structurally unreachable. Defect #1 `review_skipped` is unreachable too: it fires only when `source == "skipped-light" and draft.inferred_complexity != "light"` (validation.py:352), but `source` is set to `"skipped-light"` precisely when `complexity == "light"` (plan_reviewer.py:113-114) and the same `inferred_complexity` is what validation.py:292 passes in. The genuine silent no-op is unguarded: `except Exception: logger.debug("Plan review failed — skipping", exc_info=True)` (validation.py:307-311) leaves `review_result = None`, and `_detect_defects` guards the whole reviewer block with `if review is not None` (validation.py:348-350) — so a crashed reviewer produces zero defects and zero visible output at default log level. The class docstring still advertises 'missing dependency edges, scope imbalance warnings' as capabilities (plan_reviewer.py:1-8), and planner.py:442/454-456 renders a 'Dependencies added: N' line that is always 0.
why_it_matters: ValidationStage's own module docstring describes itself as the 'hard gate' whose review_skipped defect is 'Critical because it means the only quality gate silently no-op'd' — yet the one code path where that actually happens (reviewer raises) produces no defect and only a debug log. Two of the seven advertised detectors are dead. A maintainer reading the docstring or the `--explain` output believes structural review ran when it may not have.
proposed_fix: Delete `_apply_recommendations`, `_build_parallel_steps_from_haiku`, `_build_team_step_from_haiku`, `SplitRecommendation`, `DependencyRecommendation`, and the `dependencies_added` field (plus its `--explain` rendering) or wire them to a live path; update the PlanReviewer docstring to describe only splitting/teaming. Replace the swallowed exception at validation.py:307-311 with `logger.warning(..., exc_info=True)` plus a `PlanDefect(code="review_failed", severity="critical")` so a crashed reviewer blocks the same way a skipped one is documented to.
test_strategy: Inject a `plan_reviewer` stub whose `review()` raises; assert `ValidationStage.run` produces a defect with code `review_failed` and that `PlanQualityError` is raised under default env. Assert `"dependencies_added"` no longer appears in `PlanReviewResult` (or that a live path populates it). Static/lint test asserting `_apply_recommendations` has at least one caller, or is absent.

title: Golden plan-snapshot suite is non-hermetic and its investigative case is neutered by an explicit override
evidence: The suite calls `IntelligentPlanner()` with no `task_classifier` (test line 120), and `IntelligentPlanner.__init__` defaults to `FallbackClassifier()` (planning/planner.py:226-228), which shells out to the `claude` CLI via `TalentAgentClassifier` and only falls back to `KeywordClassifier` when that CLI is unavailable (classifier.py:805-814). Running `pytest tests/planning/test_plan_quality_golden.py` on this machine fails: `compound-multi-concern` expects `{'task_type': 'test'}` (keyword-classifier output, phases Implement/Review) but gets `{'task_type': 'new-feature'}` with phases Design/Implement/Test/Review. Separately, the one case named `investigative-bug` passes `{"task_type": "bugfix"}` (test line 77) — an explicit override, which forces `_classify_task` down the non-classifier branch (classification.py:155-181) where `task_cls` stays `None` and `draft.planning_archetype` remains `"phased"`. So the investigative archetype is never exercised end-to-end anywhere in the suite (`grep -rn investigative tests/` finds only config/unit tests over `INVESTIGATIVE_CONFIG` and the resolver's retry logic).
why_it_matters: The suite that exists to lock plan shapes fails for every developer who has the `claude` CLI installed — i.e. the project's own target audience — training maintainers to ignore it. And because its investigative case sidesteps the archetype, the total-planning-failure bug above shipped undetected: `create_plan` on any debug/RCA phrasing raises, and no test covers it.
proposed_fix: Pin the classifier in the golden fixture (`IntelligentPlanner(task_classifier=KeywordClassifier())`) so snapshots are deterministic regardless of CLI availability, and add golden cases that exercise each archetype through classification rather than through overrides — e.g. prompt 'Debug the intermittent 500 error in the checkout API' with no kwargs, asserting `plan.archetype == "investigative"`.
test_strategy: The suite must pass with and without the `claude` binary on PATH (assert this by running it once with `PATH` stripped of the CLI and once with it present). A new parametrised case per archetype must assert `plan.archetype` equals the expected value AND that `create_plan` returns rather than raising, so any future archetype whose phases fail the quality gate breaks the build.

title: Compliance hash chain is not tamper-evident: entry digest excludes prev_hash
evidence:
`_entry_hash()` (compliance.py:171-175) strips BOTH hash fields before digesting:
```python
clean = {k: v for k, v in entry.items() if k not in ("prev_hash", "entry_hash")}
canonical = json.dumps(clean, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"))
return hashlib.sha256(canonical.encode()).hexdigest()
```
So `entry_hash` is a pure function of the row's own content and commits to nothing about history. `verify_chain()` (compliance.py:407-420) then only checks positional linkage (`stored_prev != prev_hash`) plus `recomputed != stored_hash`. Editing `prev_hash` therefore never invalidates any hash. I ran this against the real module: appended 5 entries, deleted entry #2, and repointed entry #3's `prev_hash` to entry #1's `entry_hash` — `verify_chain` returned `(True, 'Chain intact — 4 entries verified.')`. I then rewrote a surviving entry's `detail` to "TAMPERED", recomputed only that row's `entry_hash` and the next row's `prev_hash` — again `(True, 'Chain intact — 4 entries verified.')`. The module docstring at compliance.py:203-206 claims "modifying any past entry breaks all subsequent hashes"; it breaks exactly one field in one adjacent row. The identical flaw propagates into `_verify_segment_chain()` in evidence bundles (evidence_bundle.py:860), which reuses `_entry_hash`.
why_it_matters: An operator who force-overrode a VETO, an agent that wrote to a regulated path, or a `--force` override row can be excised from `compliance-audit.jsonl` by deleting one line and editing one hex string in the next line. `baton compliance verify` and `baton evidence verify` both report the log as intact, and the AIBOM `chain_anchor` cross-check is only a non-fatal warning (evidence_bundle.py:649-654). Every downstream assurance claim — evidence bundles shipped to external auditors, the regulated-domain audit trail mandated by CLAUDE.md — rests on a property the code does not provide.
proposed_fix: Include `prev_hash` in the digest. Change `_entry_hash` to exclude only `entry_hash`, so `entry_hash = SHA256(canonical(content) + prev_hash)`; then any edit or deletion upstream invalidates every subsequent `entry_hash`, and repairing the chain requires recomputing the whole tail. Bump a chain-format marker (e.g. `chain_version: 2`) on new entries and teach `verify_chain` to accept v1 rows only in legacy mode, with `baton compliance rechain` migrating existing logs. Apply the same change in `_verify_segment_chain`. Additionally, make the AIBOM `chain_anchor` mismatch an error rather than a warning when the segment tail predates the anchor.
test_strategy: A regression test must build a 5-entry chain, then perform a *consistent* rewrite — delete entry k and set entry k+1's `prev_hash` to entry k-1's `entry_hash` — and assert `verify_chain()` returns `ok is False` with a message naming the divergence line. A second case must modify entry k's payload, recompute *only* entry k's `entry_hash` and entry k+1's `prev_hash`, and assert `ok is False`. A third must assert `_entry_hash({...,'prev_hash':'a'*64}) != _entry_hash({...,'prev_hash':'b'*64})` for otherwise identical content. Note that the existing `test_entry_hash_excludes_hash_fields` (tests/govern/test_audit_chain.py:58) currently enshrines the defect and must be inverted.

title: Evidence-bundle segment verification fails on any interleaved compliance log
evidence: `_build_compliance_segment()` filters the global log down to rows matching one task (evidence_bundle.py:236-244): `if entry_task == task_id: entries.append(entry)` … `return entries`, keeping "their original prev_hash/entry_hash fields intact" (docstring, line 215). `_verify_segment_chain()` then demands strict adjacency (evidence_bundle.py:852-857): `if prev_hash is not None and stored_prev != prev_hash: return False, f"Line {i}: prev_hash mismatch..."`. But `prev_hash` on a filtered row points at whatever row physically preceded it in the *global* log, which for a multi-task project is another task's entry. I ran the real builder against a log with two tasks interleaved (A,B,A,B,A,B) and got: `(False, "Line 2: prev_hash mismatch (expected 'a2359db2…', got '8b50ab1f…')")`. `verify_bundle()` turns that into a hard error (evidence_bundle.py:638-640) → `exit_code 1`. The happy-path fixture in tests/govern/test_evidence_bundle.py:188-190 writes the foreign entry first and the two task rows contiguously, so the failure mode is never exercised.
why_it_matters: `compliance-audit.jsonl` is a single shared file per project, and the `comply-record` PostToolUse hook appends a row per tool call, so entries from concurrent executions (CLAUDE.md documents `BATON_TASK_ID` for "multi-task scenarios") interleave by construction. The moment two tasks overlap, `baton evidence verify` — advertised as the CI-runnable integrity check — reports every bundle as "chain broken" even though nothing was tampered with. Operators face a permanently red gate, and the only rational response is to stop trusting or stop running it, which destroys the signal for real tampering.
proposed_fix: Stop pretending a filtered subset is a chain. Either (a) emit each task-scoped row together with a `chain_position` index and a Merkle-style inclusion proof against the recorded `chain_anchor`, or (b) keep the raw rows but have `_verify_segment_chain` verify only per-row `entry_hash` self-consistency plus monotonic `chain_position`, and verify linkage against the anchor rather than adjacency. Whichever is chosen, record in `manifest.json` that the segment is a projection, and reserve the strict-adjacency check for contiguous segments.
test_strategy: Build a compliance log with entries interleaved A,B,A,B,A,B, build an evidence bundle for task A, and assert `verify_bundle()` returns `ok is True` and `exit_code == 0` with no "chain broken" message. A paired negative test must mutate one byte of a segment row's payload and assert verification still fails.

title: A corrupt .claude/policies/<preset>.json silently disables all policy enforcement
why_it_matters: A one-character JSON typo in `.claude/policies/regulated.json` — or a half-written file from an interrupted `save_preset` — silently turns off every path_block and tool_restrict rule for HIGH/CRITICAL work, including `no_bash_on_data` and `block_secrets_dir`. Nothing fails, no gate trips, no bead is filed; the run proceeds and produces an evidence bundle that looks clean. The same edit is also a trivial deliberate bypass for anyone with repo write access. CLAUDE.md's rule "Don't add a code path that bypasses guardrails without a logged override" is violated by a code path that already exists.
proposed_fix: Make the failure explicit and fail-closed for the built-in names: on parse failure, if `name` is in `_STANDARD_PRESETS`, return the built-in preset (matching the log message) and emit a warning bead; if it is a custom-only name, raise a `PolicyLoadError` instead of returning `None`. Change the three call sites to distinguish "no policy configured" from "policy could not be loaded" — the latter must block dispatch (or force an APPROVAL) rather than continue, and `baton policy-check` must exit 2 on load failure regardless of `BATON_POLICY_FAIL_CLOSED` for a preset that was found but is unparseable.
test_strategy: Write `.claude/policies/regulated.json` containing `{invalid`, then assert (1) `PolicyEngine(policies_dir=...).load_preset("regulated")` returns the built-in regulated `PolicySet` (or raises `PolicyLoadError`), never `None`; (2) `_check_step_against_policy` for a step writing to a blocked path still yields an APPROVAL action rather than `None`; (3) `baton policy-check` fed a Write to `.env` exits non-zero / emits a deny decision rather than printing "skipping".

title: LLM plan review can de-escalate risk after governance stages, dropping the regulated preset with no override record
evidence:
`_review_plan_with_llm` runs *after* the whole planning pipeline (planner.py:312-316: `draft = self._pipeline.run(draft, services)` then `draft = self._review_plan_with_llm(draft)`), and applies a bidirectional risk override from raw model JSON (planner.py:661-672):
```python
# Apply risk override (can escalate OR de-escalate).
risk_override = data.get("risk_override")
if risk_override and risk_override in ("LOW", "MEDIUM", "HIGH"):
    override_enum = RiskLevel(risk_override)
    current_enum = draft.risk_level_enum or RiskLevel.LOW
    if override_enum != current_enum:
        draft.risk_level = risk_override
        draft.risk_level_enum = override_enum
        draft.git_strategy = select_git_strategy(override_enum).value
```
This directly contradicts the deliberate monotonic design one stage earlier, where the AI risk hint is applied as a max: "Use max(current, hint) so AI judgment can escalate but not lower" (stages/risk.py:161). Because the override lands after stage 11b policy validation (validation.py:228-233) and after required-agent selection, nothing re-derives the preset or re-adds `subject-matter-expert`/`auditor`. The downgraded value is what the executor consumes: `preset_name = _risk_level_to_preset(state.plan.risk_level)` (executor.py:1683, 7195, 4557) and the HIGH/CRITICAL pre-flight approval gate `if plan.risk_level.upper() in _HIGH_RISK_LEVELS` (executor.py:1847). No `record_override` call exists on this path (the only two call sites are `--force`, execute.py:895 and 2292).
why_it_matters: With `BATON_PLAN_REVIEW=sonnet` — which CLAUDE.md line 155 recommends "for unattended/managed-mode planning" — a single model response of `{"verdict":"NEEDS_CORRECTION","risk_override":"LOW"}` converts a CRITICAL regulated-data plan into a LOW one. Consequences: guardrail preset flips `regulated` → `standard_dev` (SME/auditor requirements and `no_bash_on_data` gone), the HIGH-risk pre-flight human approval is never injected, compliance-report generation at executor.py:4557 is skipped, and the git strategy is relaxed. The whole regulated-domain mandate in CLAUDE.md is defeated by an unreviewed LLM field, with no entry in `governance_overrides` and no bead — precisely the "code path that bypasses guardrails without a logged override" the module CLAUDE.md forbids.
proposed_fix: Make the plan-review override monotonic like the CLI risk hint: apply `max(current, override)` by `RISK_ORDINAL` so review can only escalate. If de-escalation must be supported, route it through `record_override(flag="--risk-override", justification=<review notes>)` so it lands in `governance_overrides` and the compliance chain, require an explicit opt-in env flag, refuse to lower a plan whose `classification` came from a pack or from a `regulated`/`security` preset, and re-run stage 11b policy validation plus required-agent resolution after any risk mutation.
test_strategy: Stub the review client to return `{"verdict":"NEEDS_CORRECTION","risk_override":"LOW"}` for a plan the DataClassifier scored CRITICAL, then assert the resulting `MachinePlan.risk_level` is still CRITICAL, that `_risk_level_to_preset(plan.risk_level) == "regulated"`, that phase 1 still has `approval_required=True`, and that `subject-matter-expert` and `auditor` remain in the roster. A second test must assert an escalation LOW→HIGH is still applied. If de-escalation is kept behind a flag, assert a `governance_overrides` row exists after it fires.

title: Team-mode segregation of duties relies on spoofable $USER and is bypassed entirely via the PMO API
evidence:
The team-mode self-approval guard compares two identities that both come from `_cli_actor()` (executor.py:4912-4913 for the approver, 1876/5343/7388 for the requester):
```python
def _cli_actor() -> str:
    user = os.environ.get("USER") or os.environ.get("USERNAME") or "unknown"
```
(executor.py:349-363). The guard itself (executor.py:4969-4991) is `if approval_mode == "team": … if requester and requester == actor: raise InvalidApprovalState(REASON_SELF_APPROVAL)`. So `USER=someone-else baton execute approve …` passes it. The same repo already ships the hardened alternative and documents exactly this threat: `override_log._current_actor()` / `_os_identity()` uses `pwd.getpwuid(os.geteuid()).pw_name` because "setting `USER=auditor` in the environment does NOT change the effective UID" (override_log.py:38-79). The API path is worse: `UserIdentityMiddleware` resolves the caller into `request.state.user_id` and its docstring states "enforcement of the team rule is done in the route handler" (middleware/user_identity.py:22-25), yet `approve_card` calls `engine.record_approval_result(phase_id=req.phase_id, result="approve", feedback=req.notes or "")` (pmo.py:1964-1968) — no `actor=user_id`, no `decision_source="api"` — and only reads `user_id` afterwards for the separate `approval_log` row (pmo.py:1974). The route-level mode constant `_APPROVAL_ENV = os.environ.get("BATON_APPROVAL_MODE", "local")` (pmo.py:2964) is defined and never referenced anywhere in the file.
why_it_matters: `BATON_APPROVAL_MODE=team` is documented in CLAUDE.md as the control that "disables self-approval — the approver must differ from the actor", with an explicit instruction not to special-case it away. In practice: (1) on the CLI it is defeated by one environment variable; (2) through the PMO UI/API every approval is attributed to the server process's `$USER`, so the engine compares server-user to server-user — either always tripping REASON_SELF_APPROVAL (making the documented web approval flow unusable in team mode) or, when the requester was a different shell user, letting *any* unauthenticated caller with an `X-Baton-User` header approve while the audit row names the server account. Either way the approvals recorded in `approvals.json` inside the evidence bundle attribute the decision to the wrong identity, which is exactly what an auditor reads that file to learn.
proposed_fix: Promote `override_log._current_actor()` to a shared `agent_baton/core/govern/identity.py` and use it for `_cli_actor()` so CLI approvals carry the OS-derived identity (with the existing `<os>?env=<env>` spoof tagging). In the API layer, pass the authenticated caller through: `engine.record_approval_result(..., actor=request.state.user_id, decision_source="api")` in both `approve_card` and `reject_card`, and add the route-level team check that the middleware docstring promises (approver `user_id` must differ from the card's requester/creator), using `_APPROVAL_ENV` or deleting it. In team mode, refuse to record an approval whose actor is empty or equals the server process identity.
test_strategy: (1) With `BATON_APPROVAL_MODE=team`, create a pending approval as OS user U, then call `record_approval_result` with `USER` monkeypatched to "someone-else" and assert `InvalidApprovalState(REASON_SELF_APPROVAL)` is still raised — the guard must key on effective UID, not `$USER`. (2) POST to `/api/v1/pmo/cards/{id}/approve` with header `X-Baton-User: alice` and assert the persisted `approval_results` row has `actor == "alice"` and `decision_source == "api"`. (3) In team mode, assert approving as the same `user_id` that requested the review returns 403/409 and writes no approval row.

title: Daemon auto-decisions are recorded as decision_source="human", falsifying the approval and gate audit trail
evidence:
Both recorders default the provenance field to `human`: `record_gate_result(..., decision_source: str = "human", actor: str = "")` (executor.py:3606-3615) and `record_approval_result(..., decision_source: str = "human", actor: str = "")` (executor.py:4864-4872). The daemon worker calls both without overriding it:
```python
if self._decision_manager is None:
    self._engine.record_approval_result(
        phase_id=phase_id, result="approve",
        feedback="auto-approved (no decision manager)")
```
(worker.py:600-605), and for a *human-required* gate:
```python
if self._decision_manager is None:
    self._engine.record_gate_result(
        phase_id=phase_id, passed=True,
        output="auto-approved (no decision manager)")
```
(worker.py:541-547). The dry-run loop does the same: `engine.record_approval_result(phase_id=phase_id, result="approve")` (execute.py:2055). `actor` then falls back to `_cli_actor()` (executor.py:4912-4913), stamping the daemon's OS user as the deciding human. These rows are exported verbatim into evidence bundles — `_collect_approvals` selects `decision_source, actor, rationale` (evidence_bundle.py:373-381) and `_collect_gates` selects `decision_source, actor` (evidence_bundle.py:264-267).
why_it_matters: An unattended daemon run of a HIGH-risk plan produces an evidence bundle in which `approvals.json` says a named human approved the pre-flight risk gate and `gates.json` says a human passed a human-required gate — when no person was involved. The A2 `decision_source` field exists precisely to distinguish `human` / `daemon_auto` / `api` / `policy_auto` (executor.py:4901-4903 documents those four values), and the one code path that must use `daemon_auto` uses the default instead. This is worse than a missing control: it manufactures affirmative false evidence of human oversight, which is the single claim an external auditor most relies on.
proposed_fix: Remove the misleading default — make `decision_source` a required argument on both recorders, or default it to `"unknown"` — and pass `decision_source="daemon_auto", actor="baton-daemon"` at worker.py:601 and worker.py:542, `decision_source="daemon_auto"` (or refuse to persist at all) on the dry-run path at execute.py:2055, and `decision_source="api"` on the pmo.py routes. Additionally, auto-passing a *human-required* gate when no DecisionManager is configured should fail the phase or emit a warning bead rather than silently passing; and `verify_bundle` should surface a warning when a HIGH/CRITICAL bundle contains approvals whose `decision_source != "human"`.
test_strategy: Drive `AgentWorker` with `decision_manager=None` through an APPROVAL action and a human-required GATE on a HIGH-risk plan, then assert the persisted `approval_results` and `gate_results` rows have `decision_source == "daemon_auto"` and an actor that is not a human username. Build an evidence bundle for that task and assert `approvals.json`/`gates.json` carry `daemon_auto` and that `verify_bundle` emits the no-human-oversight warning. A unit test should also assert `record_approval_result` called without `decision_source` does not silently produce `"human"`.

title: Evidence bundles ship un-redacted agent output; redaction toggle and IPv4 behaviour are undocumented or misdocumented
evidence: Redaction is wired into exactly one place — `ComplianceChainWriter.append` calls `default_redactor().redact_payload(entry)` (compliance.py:288-301). `grep -n redact agent_baton/core/govern/evidence_bundle.py agent_baton/core/govern/aibom.py` returns nothing. Yet the bundle writes raw DB text straight to disk: `_collect_verdicts` copies `"outcome": outcome_text` — full auditor/reviewer agent output — into `verdicts.json` (evidence_bundle.py:335-345), and `_collect_gates` copies `"output": r["output"] or ""` — raw gate/test stdout — into `gates.json` (evidence_bundle.py:264-273), with `approvals.json` carrying free-text `feedback`/`rationale` (evidence_bundle.py:373-381). Bundles are explicitly built for external distribution (`--tar`, "CI-runnable and network-free", module docstring lines 16-19). This breaks the module's own rule: "Don't log raw user data — route everything through `_redaction.py` first" (govern/CLAUDE.md:38). Two doc defects compound it: (a) `ComplianceChainWriter.append`'s docstring claims every string is scrubbed for "emails, SSNs, AWS keys, API tokens, JWTs, private keys, and IPv4 addresses" (compliance.py:274-276), but `Redactor.__init__` defaults to `include_ipv4: bool = False` and filters the ipv4 pattern out (_redaction.py:173, 178-181), so IPv4 is never redacted by default; (b) `BATON_REDACTION_ENABLED` — which disables compliance-log redaction wholesale (_redaction.py:259-267) — appears nowhere outside `_redaction.py` and its tests, and is absent from the root CLAUDE.md environment-variable table.
why_it_matters: A gate that runs a test suite against a regulated fixture, or a reviewer agent that quotes a failing record, puts PII or credentials into `gate_results.output` / `step_results.outcome`. Those strings are copied verbatim into a tarball that is, by design, handed to external auditors — the one artifact where a leak is guaranteed to leave the organisation. Meanwhile an operator reading the redaction docstring believes IP addresses are scrubbed when they are not, and no operator reading the documented env-var table can discover that `BATON_REDACTION_ENABLED=0` silently turns off compliance-log redaction entirely.
proposed_fix: Route every free-text field the bundle emits through `default_redactor().redact_payload()` before writing `gates.json`, `verdicts.json`, `approvals.json`, and the AIBOM — do it before `_build_manifest` so the SHA-256 inventory covers the redacted bytes (mirroring the compliance-chain design where the hashed value is the redacted one). Record `redaction_applied: true` plus the `last_counts` category tallies in `manifest.json` so verifiers can tell a redacted bundle from an un-redacted one. Fix the `append` docstring to state that IPv4 redaction is opt-in via `include_ipv4`, and add `BATON_REDACTION_ENABLED` to the root CLAUDE.md environment table with its default and its blast radius.
test_strategy: Seed `gate_results.output` and `step_results.outcome` with `AKIA0000000000000000`, `alice@example.com`, and `123-45-6789`, build a bundle, and assert none of those literals appear in any file under the bundle directory while `[REDACTED:aws_access_key]` / `[REDACTED:email]` / `[REDACTED:ssn]` do; then assert `verify_bundle()` still returns `ok is True` (proving the manifest hashes cover the redacted bytes). A doc test should assert `default_redactor().redact('10.0.0.5')` is unchanged, pinning the documented IPv4 behaviour to the implemented one.

title: DataClassifier is documented as an LLM classifier but is pure keyword matching, and its failure is silently swallowed
why_it_matters: An operator provisioning baton for regulated work sets `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` believing they have enabled AI-assisted risk classification, and reasonably expects a task like "reconcile the member ledger against the quarterly filing" to be recognised as regulated. It is not: with no matching keyword the classifier returns LOW, the preset is `standard_dev`, and the SME/auditor requirements CLAUDE.md declares mandatory never fire. The bare `except Exception: pass` means that if a pack-derived classifier raises — the exact mechanism organisations use to encode their own regulated path patterns — the plan is silently classified by keywords alone, with no bead, no warning, and no `classification_source` marker distinguishing it from a successful classification.
proposed_fix: Correct govern/CLAUDE.md:9 and 29 and the root CLAUDE.md:136 row to state that `DataClassifier` is deterministic keyword/path matching and that `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is not used by it (naming whichever component actually consumes the key). Replace the bare `except Exception: pass` at risk.py:146-147 with a logged warning plus a `baton beads create --type warning` entry and a `classification_source="keyword-fallback-after-error"` marker on the draft, so a failed classification is visible in `plan.md` rather than indistinguishable from a LOW verdict. If LLM-assisted classification is genuinely wanted, add it behind an explicit env flag with escalate-only semantics matching stages/risk.py:161.
test_strategy: Assert that with `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` set and network calls patched to raise, `DataClassifier().classify(...)` returns the identical `ClassificationResult` as with the key unset (proving the documented dependency does not exist — the doc must then match). Separately, inject a `data_classifier` whose `classify` raises, run the planning risk stage, and assert a warning is logged, a warning bead is created, and the resulting plan's `classification_source` marks the fallback rather than reporting a clean LOW.

title: Plan steps are reloaded in lexicographic step_id order, corrupting step order and making ≥10-step phases unloadable
evidence:
`_load_plan_struct` reads steps with `"SELECT * FROM plan_steps WHERE task_id = ? ORDER BY phase_id, step_id"` (sqlite_backend.py:2402). `step_id` is `TEXT NOT NULL` and the `plan_steps` DDL (schema.py:1597-1614) has no ordinal/sequence column, so intra-phase order is reconstructed by string sort. Planner-generated ids are `"<phase>.<n>"` (`step_id = f"{phase_id}.1"`, planning/stages/enrichment.py:529; `step.step_id = f"{parts[0]}.{int(parts[1]) + 1}"`, enrichment.py:701) so `"1.10" < "1.2"`. Probe against the real backend:
saved : ['1.1','1.2',...,'1.9','1.10','1.11']
loaded: ['1.1','1.10','1.11','1.2',...,'1.9']
With a normal sequential dependency chain (step `1.N` depends_on `1.N-1`) the reordered list violates `MachinePlan._validate_plan_graph_integrity` (execution.py:637-690) and the load raises outright:
`LOAD FAILED: ValidationError ... Plan-graph invariant violation: step '1.10' depends on '1.9', which is not declared as an earlier step.`
No cap on steps-per-phase exists in `agent_baton/core/engine/planning/`.
why_it_matters: A plan with 10+ steps in one phase and dependency links cannot be reloaded at all: `load_plan`/`load_execution` raise `ValidationError`, so `baton execute next/record/gate/resume` (each a fresh process that calls `engine._load_execution()`, cli/commands/execution/execute.py:1281,1466,1513) crash and the run is unrecoverable from baton.db. Without dependencies the failure is worse because it is silent: `ExecutionState.current_step_index` is an index into `phase.steps`, so a resumed run dispatches a different step than the one the engine believes it is on.
proposed_fix: Add an explicit ordinal column to `plan_steps` (e.g. `step_ordinal INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0`) in both PROJECT_SCHEMA_DDL and CENTRAL_SCHEMA_DDL plus a forward migration; write `enumerate(phase.steps)` in `_upsert_plan` and change the load query to `ORDER BY phase_id, step_ordinal`. Do the same for `plan_phases` if phase order is ever non-numeric. As a stop-gap for existing DBs, fall back to `ORDER BY phase_id, rowid` (insertion order) rather than `step_id`.
test_strategy: Save a `MachinePlan` whose single phase holds 11 steps `1.1..1.11`, each `depends_on` its predecessor; assert `load_plan()` returns a plan whose `[s.step_id for s in phases[0].steps]` equals the saved list exactly (not a sorted permutation) and that no `ValidationError` is raised. Add a second case with deliberately non-lexicographic ids (`b`, `a`, `c`) asserting insertion order is preserved.

title: Nine MachinePlan fields — including compliance_fail_closed and the goal-execution config — are silently dropped on every SQLite round-trip
evidence:
`_upsert_plan` writes only 18 plan columns (sqlite_backend.py:2216-2246) and `_load_plan_struct` reconstructs `MachinePlan(...)` from exactly those (sqlite_backend.py:2517-2536). Live probe against `SqliteStorage.save_execution` → `load_execution`:
LOSS completion_condition  before='all tests pass and docs updated' after=None
LOSS max_amend_cycles      before=7    after=3
LOSS compliance_fail_closed before=True after=None
LOSS max_retry_phases      before=2    after=0
LOSS archetype             before='research' after='phased'
LOSS complexity            before='heavy' after='medium'
LOSS classification_source before='haiku' after='keyword-fallback'
LOSS detected_stack        before='python' after=None
LOSS depends_on_task       before='t0'  after=None
All are live consumers: `if plan is not None and plan.compliance_fail_closed is not None: enabled = plan.compliance_fail_closed` (executor.py:325), `if not plan.completion_condition: return` (executor.py:3466), `max_retries = getattr(plan, "max_retry_phases", 0)` (resolver.py:445). SQLite is the only backend `get_project_storage` returns, and its docstring asserts "SQLite Phases A/B/C now reach lossless parity for ``ExecutionState``" (storage/__init__.py:67). Migration v46 (schema.py:1387) documents this exact bug class for `manager_mode` — "state.plan.manager_mode silently reset to False on every SQLite save/load round-trip" — but the remaining fields were never fixed, and tests/models/test_execution_sqlite_roundtrip.py:314 codifies the loss as expected behaviour.
why_it_matters: Every `baton execute` subcommand reloads state from baton.db, so the loss happens between actions, not just on resume. A regulated-domain plan built with `compliance_fail_closed=True` degrades to fail-open after the first CLI hop: a compliance-audit write failure logs a warning and execution continues instead of halting, exactly the behaviour the root CLAUDE.md promises can be overridden per-plan. `baton goal "<condition>"` is inert after the first process — `_maybe_round_out` returns immediately because `completion_condition` is `None` — so the documented G1 goal loop never runs. `max_retry_phases` collapses to 0, disabling investigative retry.
proposed_fix: Add the missing columns to `plans` in PROJECT_SCHEMA_DDL and CENTRAL_SCHEMA_DDL plus one additive forward migration (`complexity`, `classification_source`, `detected_stack`, `depends_on_task`, `archetype`, `max_retry_phases`, `compliance_fail_closed`, `completion_condition`, `max_amend_cycles`), or persist the non-hierarchical remainder as a single JSON blob column the way v47 did for `plan_diagnostics`; write them in `_upsert_plan` and read them back in `_load_plan_struct` with `plan_keys` fallbacks. Fix the `get_project_storage` docstring if any field is deliberately not persisted.
test_strategy: Add a parity test that iterates `MachinePlan.model_fields` and asserts every field is byte-equal after `save_plan` → `load_plan` for a plan built with non-default values everywhere, with an explicit allow-list of intentionally-unpersisted fields so a newly added field fails the gate. Separately assert `_compliance_fail_closed_enabled(loaded_plan) is True` for a plan saved with `compliance_fail_closed=True`.

title: SyncEngine watermark is rowid-based, so updated rows never re-sync and central.db reports stale execution status as a success
evidence:
`SyncTableSpec.watermark_column` defaults to `"rowid"` (sync.py:58) and `_sync_table` fetches `WHERE {watermark_column} > ?` (sync.py:410-414), advancing the watermark to `max_rowid`. `save_execution` deliberately uses an in-place upsert — "Use INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE (safe upsert) rather than INSERT OR REPLACE so that FK CASCADE children ... are NOT deleted" (sqlite_backend.py:119-121) — so the rowid never changes on update. Probe:
push1 -> rows_synced=4, errors=[]
(state.status flipped 'running' -> 'complete', saved)
push2 -> SyncResult(tables_synced=0, rows_synced=0, errors=[])
central executions: [{'project_id':'proj','task_id':'t1','status':'running'}]
project executions: [{'task_id':'t1','status':'complete'}]
The module docstring claims the opposite: "Conflict resolution: central.db is a read replica -- the project's baton.db is always authoritative. ``INSERT OR REPLACE`` overwrites any stale central row with the latest project data" (sync.py:180-183). `tests/test_sync_engine.py` has `test_second_push_only_copies_new_rows` and `test_new_rows_picked_up_after_first_sync` but no test that an *updated* row propagates.
why_it_matters: Central.db is the backing store for cross-project reporting — `QueryEngine.portfolio()` groups `executions` by `project_id, status` (queries.py:838-857) and the stalled-run query filters `status = 'running' AND updated_at < ...` (queries.py:820-833). Every execution that completes after its first sync is reported forever as `running`, so the portfolio view and stalled-run alerting are permanently wrong, and `SyncResult.success` is `True` with zero errors so nothing signals the drift. The `plans` table (also natural-PK upsert) is equally frozen at first-seen content.
proposed_fix: Change the incremental predicate from rowid to a change-marker: sync rows `WHERE rowid > ? OR updated_at > ?` and store both a rowid and a last-synced-timestamp watermark, or add a monotonically-incrementing `version`/`row_seq` column (executions already has `version`, bumped by the CAS UPDATE at sqlite_backend.py:170) and use that as `watermark_column` for upserted tables. Cheapest correct alternative: full-table `INSERT OR REPLACE` for the small natural-PK tables and keep the rowid watermark only for append-only tables (events, telemetry, trace_events).
test_strategy: Save an execution with `status='running'`, `engine.push(...)`, mutate to `status='complete'` and save, `engine.push(...)` again, then assert the central `executions` row for that `(project_id, task_id)` has `status == 'complete'`. Add the same assertion for a re-saved `plans.task_summary`.

title: CENTRAL_SCHEMA_DDL is missing the v15 team_members columns, so team_members sync fails on every push
evidence:
Migration v15 runs `ALTER TABLE team_members ADD COLUMN sub_team TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '[]';` and `... ADD COLUMN synthesis TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '';` (schema.py:449-450) and PROJECT_SCHEMA_DDL carries both, but the central mirror at schema.py:2730-2742 declares only `project_id, task_id, step_id, member_id, agent_name, role, task_description, model, depends_on, deliverables`. A fresh central.db is created at SCHEMA_VERSION=47 and therefore never runs migration 15. `_sync_table` builds `dst_insert_cols = ["project_id"] + insert_cols` from the *source* columns (sync.py:386-390). Probe with a plan containing one `TeamMember`:
Sync error for project proj table team_members: table team_members has no column named sub_team
success: False  errors: ['team_members: table team_members has no column named sub_team']
central team_members rows: 0
A systematic scan of MIGRATIONS vs both DDLs also flags `releases.deployment_profile_id` (v26) missing from CENTRAL_SCHEMA_DDL and `learning_issues.project_id` (v7) missing from PROJECT_SCHEMA_DDL.
why_it_matters: Any project that uses team steps — the composed-specialist-team feature that is central to agent-baton's pitch — can never sync its `team_members` rows to central.db. Every `baton sync` run reports partial failure and the watermark for that table never advances, so cross-project team/roster analytics in the PMO layer see zero rows forever. This is pure DDL drift that the existing anti-drift gate cannot catch because `test_project_schema_matches_migration_chain` only inspects the `executions` table (tests/models/test_execution_sqlite_roundtrip.py:881-925).
