Generalize the parity test to every table (see the test-coverage finding) so this class cannot recur.
test_strategy: Build a project DB via PROJECT_SCHEMA_DDL containing a `TeamMember` with a non-empty `sub_team`, push to a fresh central.db, and assert `result.errors == []`, `result.success is True`, and that the central `team_members` row round-trips `sub_team`/`synthesis` intact.

title: Pre-migration backup only fires for one hardcoded version, so v43/v44 DROP TABLE migrations destroy data with no backup
evidence:
`_ensure_schema` gates the backup on `_DESTRUCTIVE_MIGRATIONS = frozenset({42})` and only backs up when that set intersects the version range being applied (connection.py:138-142). Migration v43 runs `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS speculations;` and v44 runs `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS selfheal_attempts;` (schema.py:1316-1344) — both carry the note "ROLLBACK: restore the pre-migration backup created by migration_backup.backup_db() before this migration runs." Probe on a DB at version 42 holding rows in both tables:
version now: 47
speculations table exists: 0
backups on disk: []
Additionally, when the backup *is* attempted, failure is swallowed and the destructive migration proceeds regardless: `except Exception as _bak_exc: ... _logging.getLogger(__name__).warning("Pre-migration backup failed (continuing): %s", _bak_exc)` (connection.py:150-155). The directory's own CLAUDE.md states: "Migrations back up first. `migration_backup.py` runs before each migration; never bypass it."
why_it_matters: Any database already at v42 or v43 (i.e. every install that upgraded once since WP-G) that now upgrades to v47 loses the `speculations` and `selfheal_attempts` tables irreversibly, while the migration's own comment tells the operator to restore a `.bak-` file that was never written. The `scripts/restore_baton_db.sh` rollback path documented in v42 is therefore a dead procedure for the two migrations that follow it. Because the backup step also continues on failure, even a version in the set can be dropped without a snapshot when the DB is locked at that moment.
proposed_fix: Derive the destructive set programmatically — scan each `MIGRATIONS[v]` for `DROP TABLE`/`DROP COLUMN`/destructive `ALTER` and back up whenever any version in `range(current+1, target+1)` matches — instead of a hardcoded frozenset that must be hand-maintained. Make backup failure fatal for destructive ranges (raise, or require an explicit `BATON_ALLOW_UNBACKED_MIGRATION=1` escape hatch) rather than logging a warning and continuing.
test_strategy: Parametrize over every version in MIGRATIONS whose DDL contains `DROP TABLE`: seed a DB at `v-1`, open it through `ConnectionManager` at SCHEMA_VERSION, and assert `list_backups(db_path)` is non-empty and the backup still contains the dropped table. Add a test that monkeypatches `backup_db` to raise and asserts the destructive migration does not run.

title: Goal-execution counters (amend_cycles_used, goal_status, goal_checks, turn_count) are never persisted anywhere
evidence: `ExecutionState` declares `goal_checks: list[GoalCheck]`, `amend_cycles_used: int = 0`, `goal_status: str = ""`, `turn_count: int = 0` (execution.py:1437-1440), but none of the four appears in `ExecutionState.to_dict()` (execution.py:1757-1803) or `from_dict()` (execution.py:1805-1870). `grep -rn "amend_cycles_used\|goal_status\|goal_checks\|turn_count" agent_baton/core/storage/` returns zero hits — no column, no JSON blob, no child table. The executor treats them as durable run state: `remaining = plan.max_amend_cycles - state.amend_cycles_used` and `if remaining <= 0: state.goal_status = "exhausted"` (executor.py:3498-3505), `state.amend_cycles_used += 1` (executor.py:3590), and the completion summary prints `f"[{status_text}; {state.amend_cycles_used}/{state.plan.max_amend_cycles}"` (executor.py:4659-4663).
why_it_matters: Every `baton execute` subcommand is a fresh process that reloads state (`engine._load_execution()`, cli/commands/execution/execute.py:1281+), so `amend_cycles_used` reads 0 on every invocation. Once the companion `completion_condition` loss is fixed, the goal round-out budget can never be exhausted: `remaining` is always `max_amend_cycles`, the `goal_status='exhausted'` termination branch is unreachable, and a `baton goal` run amends indefinitely until `BATON_RUN_TOKEN_CEILING` or a human stops it. The `goal_checks` audit trail of evaluator verdicts is also lost, so the evidence for why a goal was declared met is not recoverable.
proposed_fix: Add `amend_cycles_used INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0`, `goal_status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT ''`, `turn_count INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0` to `executions` (both DDLs + forward migration) and wire them into the CAS UPDATE / INSERT in `save_execution` and into `load_execution`; persist `goal_checks` as a child table or a JSON column alongside the existing v37 JSON columns. Mirror all four in `ExecutionState.to_dict`/`from_dict` so the JSON export path stays faithful.
test_strategy: Save an `ExecutionState` with `amend_cycles_used=2`, `goal_status='active'`, one `GoalCheck`, and `turn_count=5`; reload via `load_execution` and assert all four survive. Add an executor-level test that drives two round-out cycles across two separate load/save pairs with `max_amend_cycles=2` and asserts the third boundary yields `goal_status == 'exhausted'` rather than another amendment.

title: Sync drops rows on IntegrityError but still advances the watermark, losing them permanently while reporting success
evidence: In `_sync_table`'s row loop the insert failure path is `except sqlite3.IntegrityError as exc: _log.debug("IntegrityError syncing %s row (rowid=%s): %s — skipping", spec.name, row_rowid, exc)` (sync.py:436-442) — a *debug*-level log, `count` not incremented — and the watermark advance is outside the `try`: `if row_rowid > max_rowid: max_rowid = row_rowid` (sync.py:444-445), followed unconditionally by `self._set_watermark(dst_conn, project_id, spec.name, max_rowid)` (sync.py:452). Nothing is appended to `SyncResult.errors`, so `SyncResult.success` (sync.py:161-163, `return len(self.errors) == 0`) stays `True`.
why_it_matters: A row rejected by a central FK or UNIQUE constraint — e.g. a `plans` row whose parent `executions` row failed to sync in the same run, or a `gate_results` row colliding on the natural-key UNIQUE index — is skipped and can never be retried, because the next push starts above its rowid. `baton sync` prints a clean success, `sync_history` records `status='success'`, and the missing data is discoverable only by enabling debug logging. This is exactly the "could this be failing silently" trap the repo's guiding principles call out.
proposed_fix: Do not advance `max_rowid` past a row that failed to insert: track the highest *contiguous successfully-synced* rowid, or collect failed rowids and re-attempt them on the next push. Promote the log to `warning` and append a structured entry to `SyncResult.errors` (or a new `rows_skipped` field surfaced by `sync_cmd.py`) so `success` reflects reality.
test_strategy: Sync a project table into a central DB pre-seeded so one source row violates a central constraint; assert (a) `result.success is False` or `result.rows_skipped == 1`, and (b) after removing the conflict and pushing again, the previously-skipped row is present in central — proving the watermark did not skip past it.

title: Schema/migration drift gate covers only the executions table, leaving three live drifts undetected
evidence:
`test_project_schema_matches_migration_chain` builds a fresh DB from `PROJECT_SCHEMA_DDL` and compares it against `self._executions_alter_columns_from_migrations()` — the helper's regex is scoped to `ALTER TABLE executions` only, and the assertion message says "PROJECT_SCHEMA_DDL is missing columns added by MIGRATIONS" while checking a single table. Running the same containment check across all tables and both DDLs surfaces drift the gate misses today:
PROJECT: v7 DRIFT learning_issues.project_id missing from PROJECT DDL
CENTRAL: v15 DRIFT team_members.sub_team missing from CENTRAL DDL
CENTRAL: v15 DRIFT team_members.synthesis missing from CENTRAL DDL
CENTRAL: v26 DRIFT releases.deployment_profile_id missing from CENTRAL DDL
The storage CLAUDE.md mandates "Schema changes require a migration. Edit `schema.py` *and* add a forward migration in `migrate.py`" and "Don't add a new table without a migration test confirming the upgrade path", but nothing enforces the reverse direction (migration column that never made it into the fresh-install DDL) beyond `executions`.
why_it_matters: Fresh installs are created directly from the DDL at SCHEMA_VERSION and never replay migrations, so any migration-only column produces two permanently different schemas depending on install age. That is precisely what breaks `team_members` sync today (separate finding). Because `_run_migrations` also silently swallows `no such table` and `duplicate column name` (connection.py:198-208) and then unconditionally stamps `UPDATE _schema_version SET version = ?` (connection.py:157), a skipped statement leaves the DB marked fully migrated — the drift is invisible at runtime until a query hits the missing column.
proposed_fix: Generalize the gate: parse every `ALTER TABLE <t> ADD COLUMN <c>` and `CREATE TABLE <t>` in `MIGRATIONS` and assert containment against both `PROJECT_SCHEMA_DDL` and `CENTRAL_SCHEMA_DDL`, with an explicit allow-list for tables intentionally dropped (v42/v43/v44) or scoped to only one database. Additionally have `_run_migrations` record skipped statements and refuse to stamp the new version when a statement was skipped for a table that the target DDL declares.
test_strategy: A single parametrized test over `(ddl_name, ddl)` that builds an in-memory DB, walks MIGRATIONS, and asserts `set()` of `(table, column)` pairs added by migrations minus an explicit allow-list is a subset of the fresh DDL's columns — the assertion must currently fail on `team_members.sub_team`, `team_members.synthesis`, `releases.deployment_profile_id`, and `learning_issues.project_id` before the schema fix and pass after.

title: Gate approve/reject never pass the HTTP caller's identity to the engine, breaking team-mode separation of duties and the approval audit actor
evidence:
`approve_gate` (pmo.py:1964) and `reject_gate` (pmo.py:2085) call the engine with only three kwargs:

```python
engine.record_approval_result(
    phase_id=req.phase_id,
    result="approve",
    feedback=req.notes or "",
)
```

The engine signature is `record_approval_result(self, phase_id, result, feedback="", decision_source="human", actor="", rationale="")` (executor.py:4864). When `actor` is empty it self-populates: `if not actor: actor = _cli_actor()` (executor.py:4917), and `_cli_actor()` returns `f"{user}@{hostname}"` built from `os.environ["USER"]` + `socket.gethostname()` of the **server process** (executor.py:349-363). The team-mode guard then compares that server-process string to the requester captured at start time, which is also `_cli_actor()` (executor.py:1876):

```python
approval_mode = os.environ.get("BATON_APPROVAL_MODE", "local").lower()
if approval_mode == "team":
    request = getattr(state, "pending_approval_request", None)
    if request is not None:
        requester = request.requester
        if requester and requester == actor:
            raise InvalidApprovalState(reason=InvalidApprovalState.REASON_SELF_APPROVAL, ...)
```

Meanwhile the route *does* resolve the real caller two statements later, but only for a side table: `user_id: str = getattr(request.state, "user_id", "local-user")` (pmo.py:1976) written into `approval_log`. The docstring at pmo.py:1931 promises "HTTPException 403: Self-approval rejected in team approval mode." The existing test pins the defect rather than the contract — tests/test_api_pmo_gates.py:313 asserts `mock_record.assert_called_once_with(phase_id=1, result="approve", feedback="Looks good")`, and the 403 test (line 601) mocks the engine to *raise*, so it never exercises identity plumbing at all.
why_it_matters: Two concrete failures depending on deployment. (a) Daemon runs as the same OS user/host that started the execution (the normal single-machine PMO setup): `actor == requester` for every API approval, so every `POST /api/v1/pmo/gates/{task_id}/approve` returns 403 `self_approval_rejected` in team mode and no human can ever approve a gate through the PMO UI. (b) Daemon runs as a different user (container/systemd as `root@box`): `actor != requester` always, so the person who requested the gate can approve their own gate through the API and the control silently never fires. In both cases the `ApprovalResult.actor` persisted into execution state (and hence into evidence bundles) is `root@box`, not the human who clicked approve, while `approval_log` records a different name — the two audit trails disagree about who approved a HIGH/CRITICAL-risk phase. `decision_source` also stays `"human"` instead of the `"api"` value the engine docstring defines.
proposed_fix: In both `approve_gate` and `reject_gate`, resolve `user_id = getattr(request.state, "user_id", "local-user")` *before* the engine call and pass it through: `engine.record_approval_result(phase_id=req.phase_id, result="approve", feedback=req.notes or "", actor=user_id, decision_source="api")`. Do the same for `reject`. Because the requester is stamped with `_cli_actor()` at start time, also normalise the two identity namespaces — either have the CLI stamp its requester from the same identity source used by the API, or store a canonical `requester_id` alongside the display string so the team-mode comparison is apples-to-apples. Reuse the already-resolved `user_id` for the `approval_log` insert so both trails carry one value.
test_strategy: Replace the assertion in tests/test_api_pmo_gates.py:313 with one that proves plumbing: patch `ExecutionEngine.record_approval_result`, POST with header `X-Baton-User: carol`, and assert the mock was called with `actor="carol"` and `decision_source="api"`. Add an end-to-end test with a real engine under `BATON_APPROVAL_MODE=team` and a `pending_approval_request(requester="alice")`: (1) POST approve as `X-Baton-User: alice` → 403 with `reason == "self_approval_rejected"`; (2) POST approve as `X-Baton-User: bob` → 200 **and** the persisted `ExecutionState.approval_results[-1].actor == "bob"` (not `$USER@$HOSTNAME`). A test that monkeypatches `USER` to an unrelated value must still see `actor == "bob"`.

title: Unauthenticated `X-Baton-User` header is trusted as the authorization identity, letting one token holder bypass team-mode approval separation
evidence:
`UserIdentityMiddleware._resolve_user_id` takes the raw header first, ahead of the only credential the API has:

```python
user_header = request.headers.get("X-Baton-User", "").strip()
if user_header:
    return user_header          # user_identity.py:89-91
# 2. Bearer token — use the token value as the user ID.
```

The docstring calls it "explicit user ID from trusted upstream proxy" (user_identity.py:9) but nothing establishes that trust — `TokenAuthMiddleware` only checks `provided == expected_token` (auth.py:93) against a single shared token, and never binds that token to a user. The spec-queue approval control then compares this attacker-controlled string against the stored submitter:

```python
actor: str = getattr(request.state, "user_id", "local-user")   # spec_queue.py:234
approval_mode: str = getattr(request.state, "approval_mode", "local")
if approval_mode == "team" and actor == draft.submitted_by:
    raise HTTPException(status_code=403, ...)
```

Reproduced against a real app (`create_app(token="s3cret")`, `BATON_APPROVAL_MODE=team`), all requests carrying the *same and only* bearer token:
- submit with `X-Baton-User: alice` → `submitted_by == "alice"`
- approve with `X-Baton-User: alice` → **403**
- approve with `X-Baton-User: alice-but-not-really` → **200**, `review.actor == "alice-but-not-really"`

`routes/specs.py:40` is worse still: `class SpecApproveRequest(BaseModel): actor: str = "local-user"` takes the approver identity straight from the request body.
why_it_matters: `BATON_APPROVAL_MODE=team` is documented in the root CLAUDE.md as "different reviewer required" and is the mechanism backing the regulated-domain guardrail. With a single shared token there is exactly one principal, so a submitter who wants their own spec approved simply changes one header value and gets a 200 plus a review record naming a person who never approved anything. Any org relying on this for compliance evidence has a forged approval trail, and there is no server-side record distinguishing the real caller from the claimed one.
proposed_fix: Stop treating `X-Baton-User` as an identity by default. Either (a) require a per-user credential — a token→user mapping so `_resolve_user_id` derives identity from the verified token and only honours `X-Baton-User` when the request arrives from a configured trusted-proxy CIDR/header (`BATON_TRUSTED_PROXY=1`), or (b) in `team` mode reject requests whose identity came from an unverified header with 401 rather than silently accepting them. Record the provenance on `request.state` (e.g. `user_id_source` in `{"token", "trusted_header", "fallback"}`) and have approval routes refuse `"fallback"`/untrusted-header identities in team mode. Delete the body-supplied `actor` field from `SpecApproveRequest` and read `request.state.user_id` instead.
test_strategy: With `create_app(token="s3cret")` and `BATON_APPROVAL_MODE=team`: submit a draft as one principal, enrich it, then POST approve with the same bearer token but a different `X-Baton-User` value, and assert the response is 401/403 — not 200 — unless trusted-proxy mode is explicitly enabled. A second test must assert that with trusted-proxy mode on the same request succeeds, so the proxy deployment stays supported. Also assert `POST /api/v1/specs/{id}/approve` ignores an `actor` field in the JSON body and records `request.state.user_id`.

title: `POST /pmo/specs/{id}/enrich` returns an unhandled 500 for any draft past `enriched` status
evidence:
The route has a 404 guard only, then calls the store unguarded:

```python
draft = store.get(spec_id)
if draft is None:
    raise HTTPException(status_code=404, ...)
...
updated = store.update_enrichment(spec_id, enrichment)   # spec_queue.py:193
```

`update_enrichment` raises a plain `ValueError`:

```python
if not draft.can_transition_to("enriched") and draft.status != "enriched":
    raise ValueError(f"Cannot enrich spec_draft in status {draft.status!r}")   # spec_draft_store.py:215-218
```

and `_VALID_TRANSITIONS` (spec_draft.py:24-30) permits `enriched` only from `submitted`, so `approved`, `bounced`, and `fired` all raise. Reproduced against a live `TestClient` with `BATON_SPEC_DRAFT_DB` isolation:

```
submit 201 submitted
enrich 200 enriched
approve 200 approved
re-enrich after approve -> 500 b'Internal Server Error'
```

The module docstring (spec_queue.py:6) advertises this route as "Synchronous re-enrich" with no documented terminal-status behaviour, and the handler docstring lists only `HTTPException 404` under Raises.
why_it_matters: The PMO Spec Queue UI exposes a re-enrich action per draft. A reviewer who clicks "Re-enrich" on an already-approved or already-fired spec — or double-clicks it after approving — gets a bare `500 Internal Server Error` with a server-side traceback instead of the structured 409 the rest of this router uses for every other lifecycle violation (approve/bounce/fire all pre-check status and return 409). It also breaks the module's own error contract, so UI code cannot distinguish "you can't do that now" from "the server is broken", and every occurrence pollutes logs as an unhandled exception.
proposed_fix: Mirror the guard style already used by `approve_spec_draft`/`bounce_spec_draft`: after the 404 check add `if draft.status not in ("submitted", "enriched"): raise HTTPException(status_code=409, detail=f"Cannot re-enrich spec draft in status '{draft.status}'; must be 'submitted' or 'enriched'.")`. Additionally wrap the `store.update_enrichment` call in `except ValueError as exc: raise HTTPException(409, str(exc)) from exc` to close the concurrent-transition race, and update the router docstring at spec_queue.py:6 to list the 409. Fix the stale in-line docstring at spec_queue.py:46 which says "honouring BATON_DB_PATH env var" while the code reads `BATON_SPEC_DRAFT_DB`.
test_strategy: In tests/api/test_specs_api.py, drive a draft through submit → enrich → approve using the `BATON_SPEC_DRAFT_DB` tmp DB, then POST `/api/v1/pmo/specs/{id}/enrich` and assert `status_code == 409` (not 500) and that the JSON detail names the current status. Add the same assertion for a `bounced` draft and for a `fired` draft, and one positive case asserting re-enrich of an `enriched` draft still returns 200.

title: Approval audit-log writes are swallowed by bare `except Exception: pass`, silently losing the cross-project approval trail
evidence:
Both gate routes insert into `approval_log` and discard every failure with no logging at all:

```python
user_id: str = getattr(request.state, "user_id", "local-user")
try:
    central_store: CentralStore = central
    central_store.execute(
        """INSERT INTO approval_log (log_id, task_id, phase_id, user_id, action, notes, created_at)
           VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)""", (...))
except Exception:
    pass          # pmo.py:1994-1995 (approve), pmo.py:2115-2116 (reject)
```

The only marker is an inline comment, "Write approval_log entry (best-effort — never block the response)". The route docstring makes the opposite promise: "The decision is also written to the ``approval_log`` table in central.db for cross-project audit visibility" (pmo.py:1914-1916), and it advertises `HTTPException 503: Compliance audit write failed (fail-closed mode)` (pmo.py:1937) — but that 503 only ever comes from the engine's `ComplianceWriteError`, never from this insert. `GET /api/v1/pmo/cards/{card_id}/approval-log` reads this same table and is what the UI renders.
why_it_matters: If `central.db` is missing the `approval_log` table (fresh install before migration), is locked by a concurrent writer, or lives on a read-only volume, every gate approval still returns `200 {"recorded": true}` while the audit row vanishes with zero logs, zero beads, and zero metrics. The board and the approval-log endpoint show an empty history for approvals that demonstrably happened. This directly contradicts the repo's own guiding principle #5 ("Could this functionality be failing silently?") on the one code path whose entire purpose is auditability, and it means `BATON_COMPLIANCE_FAIL_CLOSED=1` does not actually make the API's approval recording fail-closed.
proposed_fix: Replace `except Exception: pass` with `except Exception: _log.exception("approval_log write failed for task=%s phase=%s user=%s", task_id, req.phase_id, user_id)` at minimum, and honour the documented contract: when `BATON_COMPLIANCE_FAIL_CLOSED` is truthy (or the plan sets `compliance_fail_closed`), return the documented 503 `ComplianceWriteError`-shaped `ApprovalErrorResponse` instead of 200. When fail-open, emit a warning bead via the bead store as the root CLAUDE.md incident-handling rule requires, so the loss is visible. Apply the same treatment to the `request-review` insert at pmo.py:3022.
test_strategy: Patch `CentralStore.execute` to raise `sqlite3.OperationalError("no such table: approval_log")` and POST `/api/v1/pmo/gates/{task_id}/approve`. Assert (a) with `BATON_COMPLIANCE_FAIL_CLOSED=0` the response is 200 **and** a WARNING/ERROR record is captured by `caplog` naming the task and user; (b) with `BATON_COMPLIANCE_FAIL_CLOSED=1` the response is 503 with `error == "ComplianceWriteError"`. A regression assertion should confirm the current behaviour (200 with an empty log) fails the new test.

evidence:
`routes/specs.py` implements exactly four endpoints, per its own module docstring and confirmed by dumping the app's OpenAPI paths:

```
GET  /api/v1/specs
POST /api/v1/specs
GET  /api/v1/specs/{spec_id}
POST /api/v1/specs/{spec_id}/approve
```

The UI client calls two more:

```ts

archiveSpec(specId)      { return fetch(`${BASE_V1}/specs/${encodeURIComponent(specId)}/archive`, { method: 'POST', ... }) // client.ts:347
```

both of which throw `new Error('API ' + res.status)` on non-2xx, and both are wired to user actions in `SpecsPanel.tsx:224` (`await api.markSpecReviewed(spec.spec_id)`) and `:227` (`await api.archiveSpec(spec.spec_id)`). title: `POST /pmo/execute/{card_id}` reports 202 "launched" while discarding all worker stdout/stderr to DEVNULL
evidence:
The route spawns a fully detached execution and throws away every byte of diagnostic output:

```python
process = subprocess.Popen(
    cmd,
    cwd=str(project_root),
    stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL,
    stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL,
    start_new_session=True,
)
...
return ExecuteCardResponse(task_id=card_id, pid=process.pid, status="launched", ...)
```

`Popen` only raises `OSError` if the *fork/exec itself* fails, which is caught and mapped to 500. Anything the child fails at afterwards — an unimportable module, a rejected plan, a missing `bd` binary (the root CLAUDE.md makes `bd` mandatory: "raises `BdNotAvailable` if `bd` binary is missing"), a `BATON_TEAMS_BACKEND_STRICT` `UnknownTeamBackendError` — happens after the 202 has been returned and writes its traceback to `/dev/null`. The route docstring claims only "HTTPException 500: If the execution process fails to start."
why_it_matters: A PMO user clicks Execute, the board says `launched` with a real PID, and nothing ever happens: the card never leaves `queued`, no trace file appears, and there is no log anywhere on disk explaining why. Diagnosing it requires re-running `baton execute run` by hand outside the API. This is guiding principle #5 ("Could this functionality be failing silently?") failing on the single most consequential API action, and it also violates principle #7 — neither the user nor a Claude Code deployment has the information needed to recover.
proposed_fix: Redirect the child's streams to a per-task log file instead of DEVNULL, e.g. open `context_root / "executions" / card_id / "worker.log"` in append mode and pass that handle for both `stdout` and `stderr`; return its path in `ExecuteCardResponse` so the UI can link to it. Additionally poll once after a short grace period (or have the route check `process.poll()` before returning) so an immediate crash surfaces as a 500 with the first lines of the log rather than a false 202, and emit a `task.launch_failed` bus event when the worker dies before its first heartbeat.
test_strategy: Patch `subprocess.Popen` so the spawned command exits non-zero immediately with a known stderr string, then POST `/api/v1/pmo/execute/{card_id}`. Assert the worker log file exists under the execution directory and contains that string, and that the response either carries the log path or is a 500 naming the failure — asserting specifically that `stdout`/`stderr` were NOT `subprocess.DEVNULL` in the recorded call kwargs.
